module.title: Unit 7: Sport & Health: Sports & Adverbs of Frequency
module.objective: Talk about abilities and routines using 'can' and 'can't', name different sports, and describe everyday exercise habits.

subModules.title: Reading Mission: Sports, Abilities & How Often We Play
subModules.grammarFocus: Modal verb 'can' and 'can't' for ability; Adverbs of frequency (always, usually, often, sometimes, never)
subModules.vocabularyFocus: Sports vocabulary, adverbs of frequency, simple health and fitness words

content.summary: Welcome to your Reading Mission about sports and health! In this lesson, you will read a fun passage about young people and their favourite sports. You will learn how to understand sentences with 'can' and 'can't' to talk about abilities, and you will see adverbs of frequency like 'always', 'usually', 'often', 'sometimes', and 'never' to describe how often people do sports. By the end of this mission, you will feel confident reading simple texts about sports routines and abilities. Let's get started!

linguisticTarget.grammar: Modal verb 'can' + base verb for ability (I can swim) and 'can't' + base verb for inability (He can't play tennis). Adverbs of frequency: always, usually, often, sometimes, never — placed before the main verb.
linguisticTarget.vocabulary: Sports names (football, swimming, basketball, gymnastics, cycling, taekwondo, skateboarding, ice-skating), adverbs of frequency, and simple health words (healthy, exercise, fit, strong).
linguisticTarget.readingStrategy: Skim the passage first to understand the main topic. Then scan for key details: look for sports names, 'can'/'can't', and frequency adverbs to answer specific questions.

learningObjectives: Understand the main idea of a short A1 passage about people's sports abilities and routines.
Identify key details including which sports people can or can't do and how often they do them.
Recognize and understand adverbs of frequency (always, usually, often, sometimes, never) in context.
Distinguish between 'can' (ability) and 'can't' (inability) in reading passages.
Build confidence reading simple English texts about everyday sports and health topics.

contextWarmup.prompt: Read this sentence: 'Maria can play basketball, but she can't swim. She always plays basketball on Saturdays.' What does 'always' tell us?
options: It tells us how often Maria plays basketball.
It tells us where Maria plays basketball.
It tells us who Maria plays basketball with.
contextWarmup.explanation: 'Always' is an adverb of frequency. It tells us HOW OFTEN something happens. Maria plays basketball every Saturday — she always does it. Great job noticing this!

rules: Use 'can' + base verb to say someone has the ability to do something: 'She can swim.' 'They can play football.' The verb after 'can' never changes — no '-s', no '-ing', no 'to'.
Use 'can't' (cannot) + base verb to say someone does NOT have the ability: 'I can't do gymnastics.' 'He can't ice-skate.'
Adverbs of frequency go BEFORE the main verb: 'I always play tennis.' 'She never cycles to school.' 'We sometimes do taekwondo.'
The order from most to least frequent is: always (100%) → usually (80%) → often (60%) → sometimes (40%) → never (0%).
To ask about ability, put 'can' before the subject: 'Can you skateboard?' Answer: 'Yes, I can.' or 'No, I can't.'

commonTrap.trapTitle: Common Beginner Pitfall: Placing Adverbs of Frequency in the Wrong Position
commonTrap.explanation: Many beginners put adverbs of frequency at the wrong place in a sentence. Remember: adverbs of frequency come BEFORE the main verb but AFTER the verb 'be'. When reading, notice where 'always', 'sometimes', and 'never' appear — this helps you understand the sentence correctly.
commonTrap.wrong: I play always football. / She swims usually on Monday.
commonTrap.correct: I always play football. / She usually swims on Monday.

content.contractionsSubtitle: Observe how subjects and verbs smoothly merge in natural spoken English:

contractions.subject: They
contractions.exampleFull: They do not play tennis often.

contractions.subject: I
contractions.exampleFull: I am always ready for football practice.
contractions.exampleContracted: I'm always ready for football practice.

grammarFormulas.title: Sentence Structure with 'Can/Can't' and Adverbs of Frequency
grammarFormulas.description: Assemble and swap sentence blocks to explore affirmative, negative, and question patterns with 'can' for ability and adverbs of frequency for routines:

items.collocation: I always play football after school.
She usually swims on Wednesday mornings.
We often go to the gym together.
He sometimes plays basketball with his friends.
I never play golf. I don't like it.
She does exercise every morning to stay healthy.
Eating fruit and doing sports keep you healthy.
I practice swimming twice a week.
He plays on the school football team.
Running every day helps me stay fit.
She does taekwondo twice a week.

content.context: Three friends — Leo, Mia, and Sam — are talking about their favourite sports, what they can and can't do, and how often they exercise. Read their stories and enjoy!
content.text:
My name is Leo. I love sports! I can play football and I can swim very well. I always play football on Saturdays with my team. I usually swim on Sundays. I can't do gymnastics, but that's okay!

I'm Mia. I can do gymnastics and I can do somersaults too! I often practice gymnastics after school. I sometimes cycle to the park with my brother. I can't skateboard — it's too difficult for me! I never play golf because I think it's boring.

Hi, I'm Sam. I can do taekwondo and I can ice-skate. I usually do taekwondo twice a week. I sometimes ice-skate on Saturdays. I can't swim, so I never go to the swimming pool. I want to learn! Exercise is important because it keeps us healthy, fit, and strong.

highlights.note: Adverb of frequency meaning 100% of the time — placed before the main verb 'play'.
Adverb of frequency meaning most of the time (~80%) — placed before the main verb.
Adverb of frequency meaning many times (~60%) — placed before the main verb 'practice'.
Adverb of frequency meaning not always but not rarely (~40%) — placed before the main verb.
Adverb of frequency meaning 0% of the time — placed before the main verb. Notice: no 'not' needed with 'never'.
'Can' + base verb shows ability. Leo has the ability to play football.
'Can't' + base verb shows inability. Mia does not have the ability to skateboard.
A sport where you do jumps, flips, and balance exercises.
A movement where you roll your body forward or backward in a full circle.
In good physical condition; not sick. Exercise helps you stay healthy.

gistQuestion.prompt: What is the passage mainly about?
options: Three friends talking about their sports abilities and how often they exercise.
Three friends cooking dinner together at home.
Three friends planning a holiday trip to the beach.
gistQuestion.explanation: The passage is about Leo, Mia, and Sam. They talk about which sports they can and can't do, and how often they do them. This is the main idea of the text. Well done!

detailQuestions.prompt: When does Leo always play football?
detailQuestions.explanation: The passage says: 'I always play football on Saturdays with my team.' So Leo plays football on Saturdays. The word 'always' tells us he does this every Saturday.
Mia says: 'I can't skateboard — it's too difficult for me!' She CAN do gymnastics and she CAN cycle, but she CANNOT skateboard.

detailQuestions.prompt: Why does Sam never go to the swimming pool?
options: Because the pool is too far away.
detailQuestions.explanation: Sam says: 'I can't swim, so I never go to the swimming pool.' The reason is clear — he doesn't have the ability to swim. He wants to learn though!

detailQuestions.prompt: How often does Mia practice gymnastics?
options: She often practices gymnastics after school.
She always practices gymnastics on Saturdays.
detailQuestions.explanation: The passage says: 'I often practice gymnastics after school.' The adverb 'often' means she does it many times, and 'after school' tells us when.

questions.question: According to the passage, which TWO sports can Leo do?
questions.explanation: Leo says: 'I can play football and I can swim very well.' These are the two sports he can do. He also mentions he can't do gymnastics.

questions.question: In the sentence 'I always play football on Saturdays', where is the adverb of frequency placed?
options: At the end of the sentence
questions.explanation: Adverbs of frequency (always, usually, often, sometimes, never) are placed BEFORE the main verb. Here, 'always' comes before 'play'. This is the correct position in English.

questions.question: Why does Mia never play golf?
questions.explanation: Mia says: 'I never play golf because I think it's boring.' She gives a clear reason — she finds golf boring. Notice how 'never' is placed before the verb 'play'.

questions.question: How often does Sam do taekwondo?
questions.explanation: Sam says: 'I usually do taekwondo twice a week.' The adverb 'usually' means most of the time, and 'twice a week' tells us exactly how often — two times per week.

questions.question: Which sentence uses 'can't' correctly based on the passage?
questions.explanation: Sam clearly says: 'I can't swim, so I never go to the swimming pool.' He CAN do taekwondo and he CAN ice-skate, but he CANNOT swim.

questions.question: Read this sentence from the passage: 'Exercise is important because it keeps us healthy, fit, and strong.' What does 'fit' mean here?
options: In good physical condition and active
questions.answer: In good physical condition and active
questions.explanation: 'Fit' in this context means being in good physical condition because of regular exercise. Sam is saying that exercise helps our bodies stay healthy, active, and strong.

questions.question: Which adverb of frequency means 'zero percent of the time'?
questions.explanation: 'Never' means 0% — it means you do NOT do something at any time. For example, 'I never play golf' means 'I do not play golf at any time.' Remember: when you use 'never', you don't need 'not' in the sentence.

questions.question: Choose the sentence that has the adverb of frequency in the CORRECT position.
options: She sometimes cycles to the park.
She cycles sometimes to the park.
Sometimes cycles she to the park.
questions.answer: She sometimes cycles to the park.
questions.explanation: The correct position for adverbs of frequency is BEFORE the main verb. 'She sometimes cycles to the park' follows this rule perfectly — 'sometimes' comes before 'cycles'. Great reading!

subModules.title: Listening Mission: Sports Talk — What Can You Do?

content.summary: In this listening mission, you will hear two friends talking about sports they can and cannot do. They also talk about how often they do sports using words like 'always', 'usually', 'sometimes', and 'never'. Listen carefully for the words 'can' and 'can't' — they sound very similar in fast speech! Also pay attention to adverbs of frequency, which tell you how often someone does something. A useful strategy is to listen for the main verb after 'can' or 'can't' to understand what sport the speaker is talking about.
learningObjectives: Identify sports vocabulary such as 'basketball', 'swimming', 'football', and 'yoga' in spoken English.
Distinguish between 'can' and 'can't' in natural spoken sentences.
Recognise adverbs of frequency ('always', 'usually', 'sometimes', 'often', 'never') when listening to descriptions of sports routines.
Understand simple questions and answers about ability and habits related to sport and health.

keyPhrases.note: Used to ask about someone's ability to do a sport. The verb after 'play' is usually a ball sport like basketball or football.
Used to say you do not have the ability to do something. Listen for the /t/ sound at the end of 'can't' to tell it apart from 'can'.
'Usually' means about 80% of the time. It comes before the main verb in a sentence.
This question asks about frequency. Common answers use adverbs like 'always', 'sometimes', or 'never'.

keyPhrases.phrase: I sometimes play football after school.
keyPhrases.meaning: Aku kadang-kadang bermain sepak bola setelah sekolah.
keyPhrases.note: 'Sometimes' means about 50% of the time. It can go at the beginning or middle of a sentence.
A time expression used to describe a regular habit. It usually goes at the end of a sentence.

connectedSpeech.note: In fast speech, 'can' reduces to a very short /kən/ and 'you' becomes /jə/. The vowel in 'can' almost disappears. This is why it can be hard to hear the difference between 'can' and 'can't'.

In natural speech, 'cannot' becomes 'can't'. The vowel in 'can't' is longer /ɑː/ and there is often a glottal stop instead of a clear /t/ at the end. This longer vowel helps you hear the difference from 'can' /kən/.
In fast speech, 'usually' loses a syllable and sounds like 'yoozhly'. The final '-ing' in 'swimming' often becomes '-in' in casual speech.
'That is' contracts to 'that's' in natural speech. The /ɪz/ sound disappears and becomes just /s/ attached to 'that'.

sections.title: Audio Dialogue: Talking About Sports at the Park

content.context: Alex and Jamie are sitting on a bench at the park after school. They see people playing different sports around them. They start talking about which sports they can do and how often they do them.
content.audioPrompt: Listen carefully to the following dialogue between two friends, Alex and Jamie. Pay attention to the sports they mention, whether they can or cannot do them, and how often they practise.

lines.speaker: Alex
lines.text: Hey Jamie! Look, those people are playing basketball. Can you play basketball?
lines.translation: Hei Jamie! Lihat, orang-orang itu sedang bermain basket. Bisakah kamu bermain basket?

lines.speaker: Jamie
lines.text: Yes, I can! I play basketball every weekend with my brother.
lines.translation: Ya, aku bisa! Aku bermain basket setiap akhir pekan dengan kakakku.

lines.speaker: Alex
lines.text: That's great! How often do you play?
lines.translation: Bagus sekali! Seberapa sering kamu bermain?

lines.speaker: Jamie
lines.text: I usually play twice a week. What about you? Can you play basketball?
lines.translation: Aku biasanya bermain dua kali seminggu. Bagaimana denganmu? Bisakah kamu bermain basket?

lines.speaker: Alex
lines.text: No, I can't. But I can play football. I sometimes play football after school.
lines.translation: Tidak, aku tidak bisa. Tapi aku bisa bermain sepak bola. Aku kadang-kadang bermain sepak bola setelah sekolah.

lines.speaker: Jamie
lines.text: Nice! Can you do taekwondo too? I see a taekwondo class over there.
lines.translation: Keren! Bisakah kamu juga melakukan taekwondo? Aku melihat kelas taekwondo di sana.

lines.speaker: Alex
lines.text: No, I can't do taekwondo. I never do martial arts. Can you swim?
lines.translation: Tidak, aku tidak bisa taekwondo. Aku tidak pernah melakukan seni bela diri. Bisakah kamu berenang?

lines.speaker: Jamie
lines.text: Yes, I can swim very well! I always go swimming on Monday mornings. It's good for my health.
lines.translation: Ya, aku bisa berenang dengan sangat baik! Aku selalu pergi berenang pada Senin pagi. Itu baik untuk kesehatanku.

lines.speaker: Alex
lines.text: I sometimes go swimming too, but I'm not very good. Do you do yoga?
lines.translation: Aku kadang-kadang pergi berenang juga, tapi aku tidak terlalu pandai. Apakah kamu melakukan yoga?

lines.speaker: Jamie
lines.text: Yes! I often do yoga at home. It helps me relax after sport. You should try it!
lines.translation: Ya! Aku sering melakukan yoga di rumah. Itu membantuku rileks setelah olahraga. Kamu harus mencobanya!

subModules.title: Writing Mission: Sports I Can Do & My Exercise Habits

content.summary: In this lesson, you will learn how to write sentences and short paragraphs about sports you can and can't do, and how often you do them. You will use 'can' and 'can't' with sport verbs, and adverbs of frequency like 'always', 'usually', 'sometimes', 'often', and 'never'. Remember: after 'can', always use the base verb (no 'to', no '-s'). Let's build your writing step by step!

blueprintItems.title: Add How Often You Do a Sport
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + adverb of frequency + base verb + sport/object.
blueprintItems.example: I usually play football on Saturdays.

blueprintItems.title: Combine Ability and Frequency in a Paragraph
blueprintItems.example: I can swim. I always swim on Sundays. I love swimming!

mechanicsRules.rule: Always use the base verb after 'can' or 'can't'. Do not add '-s', '-ing', or 'to'.
mechanicsRules.why: After 'can', the verb never changes. It stays in its base form for all subjects: I, you, he, she, it, we, they.

mechanicsRules.rule: Start every sentence with a capital letter and end with a period (.) or question mark (?).
mechanicsRules.why: Every English sentence must begin with a capital letter. Questions end with a question mark (?), and statements end with a period (.).

mechanicsRules.rule: Place adverbs of frequency (always, usually, often, sometimes, never) before the main verb but after the subject.
mechanicsRules.why: In English, adverbs of frequency come between the subject and the main verb. This is the correct word order.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use 'can't' (with an apostrophe) as the short form of 'cannot'. Do not write 'cannt' or 'can not' as one word with a space.
mechanicsRules.why: The correct contraction is 'can't' with an apostrophe replacing the letters 'no' in 'cannot'.

sampleSentences.focus: Question form with 'Can' + subject + base verb

sampleSentences.id: Saya biasanya pergi jogging di pagi hari.
sampleSentences.focus: Adverb of frequency 'usually' before main verb

sampleSentences.id: Mereka tidak pernah bermain tenis pada hari Senin.

practicumQuestions.criteria: Includes at least 2 sentences with 'can' about sports at school. Includes at least 1 sentence with 'can't'. Includes at least 1 sentence with an adverb of frequency. The message is friendly and clear. All sentences start with capital letters and end with correct punctuation. Uses base verbs after 'can/can't'.
practicumQuestions.sampleGoodAnswer: Hi! At my school, I can play basketball. I can also swim in the school pool. I can't play tennis because we don't have a tennis court. I usually play basketball on Wednesdays and Fridays. It is my favourite sport!

subModules.title: Speaking Lab: Sports I Can Do & My Exercise Habits

content.summary: In this speaking lab, you will practise talking about sports you can and cannot do, and how often you do them. You will learn to pronounce sport names clearly, use 'can' and 'can't' with the correct stress, and say adverbs of frequency like 'always', 'usually', 'sometimes', and 'never' with natural rhythm. Good pronunciation of 'can' /kæn/ (weak, unstressed) versus 'can't' /kænt/ (strong, stressed) is very important because they sound very similar to listeners.
content.audioGuidance: Pay attention to stress patterns: in positive sentences, 'can' is usually weak and short — /kən/. In negative sentences, 'can't' is strong and clear — /kænt/. For adverbs of frequency, stress the first syllable: AL-ways, U-su-al-ly, SOME-times, NEV-er. When asking questions like 'Can you swim?', use rising intonation at the end. When answering 'I can swim' or 'I can't swim', use falling intonation.

pillars.name: Can vs. Can't Clarity
pillars.target: Clear distinction between 'can' and 'can't' in speech
pillars.explanation: In fast speech, 'can' becomes weak: /kən/. But 'can't' stays strong: /kænt/. The vowel sound and the final /t/ help listeners know which word you mean. Practise saying 'I can swim' (short, weak 'can') and 'I can't swim' (long, strong 'can't' with a clear /t/ sound).

pillars.name: Sport Vocabulary Pronunciation
pillars.target: Accurate pronunciation of common sport names
pillars.explanation: Many sport words have two syllables with stress on the first: FOOT-ball, TEN-nis, BAS-ket-ball, SWIM-ming. Some have one syllable: golf, bike. Say each sport name slowly first, then faster. Make sure the stressed syllable is louder and longer.

pillars.name: Frequency Adverb Rhythm
pillars.target: Natural rhythm when using adverbs of frequency in sentences
pillars.explanation: Adverbs of frequency go before the main verb: 'I always play football.' 'She never swims.' Stress the adverb and the main verb: 'I AL-ways PLAY football.' This creates a natural English rhythm that is easy to understand.

pillars.name: Question Intonation for Ability
pillars.target: Rising intonation in yes/no questions with 'can'
pillars.explanation: When you ask 'Can you play tennis?', your voice should go UP at the end. This rising intonation tells the listener it is a question. When you answer 'Yes, I can' or 'No, I can't', your voice goes DOWN at the end.

stressPairs.shiftExplanation: Both 'football' and 'basketball' stress the first syllable. Notice that 'basketball' has three syllables but the stress stays at the front: BAS-ket-ball. Keep the first syllable loud and clear.
Notice the stress shift: 'always' has stress on the FIRST syllable (AL-ways), but 'sometimes' has stress on the SECOND syllable (some-TIMES). This difference is important for natural rhythm.

'Usually' has four syllables with stress on the first: U-su-al-ly. 'Never' has two syllables, also stressed on the first: NEV-er. Both stress the first syllable, but 'usually' is much longer — practise keeping it smooth.
Both 'exercise' and 'volleyball' have three syllables with stress on the first. Say the first syllable louder: EX-er-cise, VOL-ley-ball. Keep the other syllables short and soft.

drills.hint: Say 'can' quickly and softly — like 'kən'. Do not stress it. Stress 'play' and 'football' instead.
Say 'can't' with a strong vowel /æ/ and a clear /t/ at the end. Make it longer and louder than 'can'.
Let your voice rise on the word 'swim'. This tells the listener you are asking a question.

drills.targetText: I always play basketball on Monday.
drills.focus: Adverb of frequency placement and stress
drills.hint: Stress 'AL-ways' and 'PLAY' and 'BAS-ket-ball'. The adverb 'always' comes before the verb 'play'.

drills.targetText: She sometimes goes swimming after school.
drills.hint: Stress the second syllable of 'sometimes': some-TIMES. Then stress 'SWIM-ming' and 'SCHOOL'.

drills.targetText: I usually ride my bike twice a week.
drills.phonetic: /aɪ ˈjuː.ʒu.ə.li raɪd maɪ baɪk twaɪs ə wiːk/
drills.hint: Say 'usually' as four syllables: U-su-al-ly. Stress the first syllable. For 'twice', make sure you say the /tw/ clearly.

roleplay.context: You are at a sports centre. Mr. Khoirul is a friendly sports coach. He wants to know what sports you can do and how often you exercise. Answer his questions using 'can', 'can't', and adverbs of frequency.

turns.speaker: Mr. Khoirul
turns.text: Hello! Welcome to the sports centre. Tell me, what sports can you do?
turns.translation: Halo! Selamat datang di pusat olahraga. Ceritakan, olahraga apa yang bisa kamu lakukan?

turns.speaker: Student
turns.text: I can play football and I can swim.
turns.translation: Saya bisa bermain sepak bola dan saya bisa berenang.

turns.speaker: Mr. Khoirul
turns.text: That's wonderful! Can you play tennis too?
turns.translation: Bagus sekali! Bisakah kamu bermain tenis juga?

turns.speaker: Student
turns.text: No, I can't play tennis, but I can ride a bike.
turns.translation: Tidak, saya tidak bisa bermain tenis, tapi saya bisa naik sepeda.

turns.speaker: Mr. Khoirul
turns.text: Great! How often do you play football?
turns.translation: Bagus! Seberapa sering kamu bermain sepak bola?

turns.speaker: Student
turns.text: I usually play football twice a week, on Tuesday and Thursday.
turns.translation: Saya biasanya bermain sepak bola dua kali seminggu, pada hari Selasa dan Kamis.

turns.speaker: Mr. Khoirul
turns.text: And how often do you swim?

turns.speaker: Student
turns.text: I sometimes swim on Saturday morning.
turns.translation: Saya kadang-kadang berenang pada hari Sabtu pagi.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Tell a short story about the sports you can do and how often you do them. Use the three story points below to guide your answer. Speak for about 30 seconds.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Now, please tell me a short story about the sports you can do. Talk about what sports you like, how often you do them, and one sport you cannot do.
storyPoints: Talk about two or three sports you can do, for example: football, swimming, or basketball.
Say how often you do each sport using adverbs of frequency like 'always', 'usually', 'sometimes', or 'twice a week'.
Mention one sport you cannot do and say you want to learn it.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: I can play football and I can swim. I usually play football three times a week. I sometimes swim on Sunday. I can't play tennis, but I want to learn.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /aɪ kən pleɪ ˈfʊt.bɔːl ənd aɪ kən swɪm. aɪ ˈjuː.ʒu.ə.li pleɪ ˈfʊt.bɔːl θriː taɪmz ə wiːk. aɪ sʌmˈtaɪmz swɪm ɒn ˈsʌn.deɪ. aɪ kænt pleɪ ˈten.ɪs bʌt aɪ wɒnt tuː lɜːn/
practicumQuestions.hint: Remember to use weak 'can' /kən/ in positive sentences and strong 'can't' /kænt/ in negative sentences. Use falling intonation for statements.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This storytelling task tests your ability to combine sport vocabulary with 'can/can't' and adverbs of frequency in a natural, connected monologue. Good speakers link their ideas smoothly.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Tell a short story about your weekly exercise routine. Describe what you do on different days and how it makes you feel. Use the three story points below.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Please tell me about your exercise routine during the week. What do you do? When do you do it? How does it make you feel?
storyPoints: Describe what exercise or sport you do on specific days of the week.
Use adverbs of frequency to explain your habits, for example: 'I always run on Monday' or 'I never play golf'.
Say how exercise makes you feel, for example: 'I feel happy' or 'I feel strong'.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: I always run on Monday and Wednesday. I sometimes ride my bike on Friday. I never play golf. Exercise makes me feel happy and strong.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /aɪ ˈɔːl.weɪz rʌn ɒn ˈmʌn.deɪ ənd ˈwenz.deɪ. aɪ sʌmˈtaɪmz raɪd maɪ baɪk ɒn ˈfraɪ.deɪ. aɪ ˈnev.ər pleɪ ɡɒlf. ˈek.sə.saɪz meɪks miː fiːl ˈhæp.i ənd strɒŋ/
practicumQuestions.hint: Stress the adverbs of frequency: AL-ways, some-TIMES, NEV-er. Use falling intonation at the end of each statement.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This task practises organising a short monologue about daily routines using time expressions and frequency adverbs. It builds fluency for real-life conversations about health habits.

practicumQuestions.instruction: You are calling a sports centre to ask about classes. Mr. Khoirul is the receptionist. Ask what classes are available and tell him what sports you can do.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Ring ring! Hello, this is the Happy Sports Centre. My name is Mr. Khoirul. How can I help you today?
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You are a new student calling the Happy Sports Centre. You want to join a sports class. You can play football and swim, but you cannot play badminton. Ask Mr. Khoirul about class times and days.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: Mr. Khoirul is a friendly receptionist at the sports centre. He answers your questions about classes, days, and times. He speaks slowly and clearly.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Hello! I want to join a sports class. I can play football and I can swim. Can I join the swimming class? How often is the class?
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /həˈləʊ. aɪ wɒnt tuː dʒɔɪn ə spɔːts klɑːs. aɪ kən pleɪ ˈfʊt.bɔːl ənd aɪ kən swɪm. kæn aɪ dʒɔɪn ðə ˈswɪm.ɪŋ klɑːs. haʊ ˈɒf.ən ɪz ðə klɑːs/
practicumQuestions.hint: Use rising intonation when asking questions: 'Can I JOIN the class?' and 'How OFTEN is the class?'
practicumQuestions.explanation: This roleplay practises making enquiries on the phone using 'can' for ability and 'how often' for frequency. It simulates a real-world situation where you need to communicate your sports abilities.

practicumQuestions.instruction: You meet Mr. Khoirul at school. He is your PE teacher. He asks you about your sports abilities and exercise habits. Answer his questions honestly.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Good morning! I am your new PE teacher, Mr. Khoirul. I want to know about your sports skills. Let's talk!
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: It is the first day of PE class at school. Mr. Khoirul, the PE teacher, wants to learn about each student's abilities. He will ask you what sports you can and cannot do, and how often you exercise.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: Mr. Khoirul is a kind and encouraging PE teacher. He asks simple questions about your sports abilities and exercise routine. He gives positive feedback.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Good morning, Mr. Khoirul! I can play basketball and I can run fast. I can't play volleyball. I usually exercise three times a week.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ɡʊd ˈmɔː.nɪŋ ˈmɪs.tər kɔɪ.rʊl. aɪ kən pleɪ ˈbɑːs.kɪt.bɔːl ənd aɪ kən rʌn fɑːst. aɪ kænt pleɪ ˈvɒl.i.bɔːl. aɪ ˈjuː.ʒu.ə.li ˈek.sə.saɪz θriː taɪmz ə wiːk/
practicumQuestions.hint: When Mr. Khoirul asks a yes/no question, answer with 'Yes, I can' or 'No, I can't' first, then add more details.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This roleplay simulates a common school situation. You practise answering questions about ability and frequency, which is essential for everyday English communication.

practicumQuestions.instruction: You are talking to Mr. Khoirul, your friend, about weekend plans. Discuss what sports you want to do together this weekend.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Hey! It's the weekend tomorrow! I want to do some sports. Do you want to come with me? What can you do?
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: It is Friday afternoon. Mr. Khoirul calls you to make weekend plans. He wants to play sports together. You need to discuss what sports you both can do and decide on a time.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: Mr. Khoirul is your friendly classmate. He is excited about the weekend and wants to do sports with you. He suggests different activities and asks about your preferences.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Yes, I want to play sports! I can play football. Can you play football too? Let's play on Saturday morning. I always play in the park.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /jes aɪ wɒnt tuː pleɪ spɔːts. aɪ kən pleɪ ˈfʊt.bɔːl. kæn juː pleɪ ˈfʊt.bɔːl tuː. lets pleɪ ɒn ˈsæt.ə.deɪ ˈmɔː.nɪŋ. aɪ ˈɔːl.weɪz pleɪ ɪn ðə pɑːk/
practicumQuestions.hint: Use 'can' to talk about ability and 'always' or 'usually' to talk about your habits. Ask questions with rising intonation.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This roleplay practises making plans with a friend using ability language and frequency adverbs. It is a very common real-life speaking situation for A1 learners.

practicumQuestions.instruction: You visit a doctor, Mr. Khoirul. He asks about your exercise habits and health. Tell him what sports you do and how often.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Hello, please sit down. I am Doctor Khoirul. I want to ask you some questions about your health and exercise. Is that okay?
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You are visiting Doctor Khoirul for a health check-up. He wants to know about your exercise habits to give you health advice. You need to tell him what sports you do, how often, and if there are sports you cannot do.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: Mr. Khoirul is a friendly doctor. He asks simple questions about your exercise and health habits. He gives you advice based on your answers.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Hello, Doctor. I usually swim twice a week and I sometimes run in the morning. I can't play tennis because my arm hurts. I always try to exercise.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /həˈləʊ ˈdɒk.tər. aɪ ˈjuː.ʒu.ə.li swɪm twaɪs ə wiːk ənd aɪ sʌmˈtaɪmz rʌn ɪn ðə ˈmɔː.nɪŋ. aɪ kænt pleɪ ˈten.ɪs bɪˈkɒz maɪ ɑːm hɜːts. aɪ ˈɔːl.weɪz traɪ tuː ˈek.sə.saɪz/
practicumQuestions.hint: Speak clearly and slowly, like you are talking to a real doctor. Use 'usually', 'sometimes', and 'always' to describe your habits.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This roleplay practises a health-related conversation, combining sports vocabulary with frequency adverbs and 'can/can't'. Talking to a doctor about exercise is a practical life skill.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say the following sentence out loud. Focus on pronouncing each sport name clearly and correctly.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Please say this sentence clearly. Pay attention to the sport words.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: I can play football, basketball, and volleyball, but I can't play badminton.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /aɪ kən pleɪ ˈfʊt.bɔːl ˈbɑːs.kɪt.bɔːl ənd ˈvɒl.i.bɔːl bʌt aɪ kænt pleɪ ˈbæd.mɪn.tən/
practicumQuestions.hint: Stress the first syllable of each sport: FOOT-ball, BAS-ket-ball, VOL-ley-ball, BAD-min-ton. Say each word separately first, then say the full sentence.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This drill tests your pronunciation of four common sport names. All four words stress the first syllable. Clear pronunciation of sport vocabulary is essential for being understood when talking about your hobbies.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say the following sentences out loud. Focus on the correct use of 'can', 'can't', and the adverb of frequency in the right position.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Please say these two sentences. Be careful with the grammar: where does the adverb go?
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: I can always play football on Monday. She can never swim in the evening.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /aɪ kən ˈɔːl.weɪz pleɪ ˈfʊt.bɔːl ɒn ˈmʌn.deɪ. ʃiː kən ˈnev.ər swɪm ɪn ðə ˈiːv.nɪŋ/
practicumQuestions.hint: The adverb of frequency goes AFTER 'can' and BEFORE the main verb: 'can always play', 'can never swim'. Do not put the adverb before 'can'.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This drill practises the correct word order when combining modal 'can' with adverbs of frequency. The pattern is: Subject + can + adverb + verb. This is a key grammar point for A1 learners.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say the following words and sentence. Focus on which syllable is stressed in each word. The stressed syllable is shown in CAPITAL letters.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Listen and repeat. Pay attention to the stressed syllable in each word: EX-er-cise, U-su-al-ly, bad-MIN-ton. Now say the full sentence.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: I usually do exercise and sometimes play badminton.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /aɪ ˈjuː.ʒu.ə.li duː ˈek.sə.saɪz ənd sʌmˈtaɪmz pleɪ ˈbæd.mɪn.tən/
practicumQuestions.hint: Stress pattern: U-su-al-ly (first syllable), EX-er-cise (first syllable), some-TIMES (second syllable), BAD-min-ton (first syllable). Make the stressed syllable louder and longer.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This drill focuses on syllable stress in multi-syllable words related to sports and frequency. Notice that most words stress the first syllable, but 'sometimes' stresses the second. Getting stress right makes your English much easier to understand.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say the following question and answer pair. Use RISING intonation for the question and FALLING intonation for the answer.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Say the question with your voice going UP at the end. Then say the answer with your voice going DOWN at the end.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Can you play tennis? No, I can't play tennis, but I can always ride my bike.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /kæn juː pleɪ ˈten.ɪs ↗ | nəʊ aɪ kænt pleɪ ˈten.ɪs bʌt aɪ kən ˈɔːl.weɪz raɪd maɪ baɪk ↘/
practicumQuestions.hint: For the question 'Can you play tennis?', let your voice RISE on 'tennis?' — go up like climbing stairs. For the answer, let your voice FALL at the end on 'bike.' — go down like going down stairs.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This drill practises the essential difference between rising intonation (for yes/no questions) and falling intonation (for statements). In English, intonation carries meaning: rising = question, falling = statement or certainty. Mastering this makes your speech sound natural.
